name: Tettenhall Yews

location.address: St Michael and All Angels churchyard, Upper Street, Tettenhall, Wolverhampton WV6

access: Free. Open parish churchyard; the ground on the north side slopes steeply.
transport: Tettenhall village, about three miles west of Wolverhampton city centre by bus; the churchyard is beside the village green.

location_site.name: St Michael and All Angels churchyard, north side

how_to_recognise: You can recognise them as the three old yews in a line on the steep north side of the church. The biggest, nearest the church, has a fire-scarred split trunk; the middle one is a hollow, burnt-out shell with ivy.

photo.note: No usable photo found. Two Commons/Geograph files titled 'Yew tree, St Michael's Churchyard' (1821508, 2834245) are geotagged at 51.19N 1.61W in Hampshire, NOT Tettenhall; do not use. Commons has geograph churchyard views within 40 m (e.g. 7864664 by ElfExplorer, 2024, CC BY-SA 2.0; 408902 by John M, 2007) but their titles do not name the yews and they were not viewed (image fetch rate-limited), so unchecked. Ancient Yew Group photos (Tim Hills) are copyright.

verify_notes: Ancient Yew Group (AYG) site record, visited 9 June 1999 by Tim Hills, photos 2012. Churchyard of St Michael and All Angels, Lichfield diocese, grid ref SJ89110031, coordinates 52.600468 -2.1622183 are the site-level map link, not a tree fix. Three yews in a line on the north side: two male, one female (AYG notes; the database does not assign sex per ID, except tree 3874 listed as male). Tree 784: class Ancient 7m+, closest to the church, no girth in database; the 2019 site file says the ancient male's growth area splits into four branches, a limb strains the bole, a new stem has emerged from the base, girth 22 ft 9 in at 1 ft (about 693 cm) in 1999. Tree 3874: Ancient 5-7m, middle one, slightly smaller male, 'burnt out hollow shell' on steeply sloping ground, hollow closes over above head height, ivy up into the canopy (Tim Hills, 7 April 2012); earliest mention 1804, Gentleman's Magazine. Tree 785: Ancient 5-7m, furthest from church, female, a series of branches around the truncated centre of the original tree, girth 22 ft 4 in (681 cm) at the base in 1999. Each of the three showed fire or smoke damage in 1999. History cited in the AYG file: 'venerable yew-trees' noted 1804; Gardener's Chronicle 1874 reported all three, the most bulky 24 ft in girth; in 1899 the North Staffs Field Club visit recorded a Mr Collins of Trentham pronouncing the great yew 'more than 2,000 years' old. That 2,000 year figure is a century-old opinion and is NOT adopted; no modern age basis, so age left empty. Church mostly rebuilt after a fire in 1950 (only the 1883 decorated tower and porch survive), so the yews are older than the present church. Alive: AYG photos from 2012 and a visit note for 2019 site file (copyright 2019); no photo from the last three years was seen, so flagged. Sources are one society database plus its historical citations; the churchyard is owned by the PCC. Treat the three as one collectible point (one place to stand). Girth_cm uses the larger 1999 figure for tree 784 (693 cm), 785 is 681 cm; the two are different measurement heights (1 ft vs base).
story:
The parish church of Tettenhall burned in 1950 and was rebuilt, keeping only its tower and porch. The three yews on the north side of the churchyard were already called venerable in 1804, so they are older than nearly everything in the building they stand beside.

The Ancient Yew Group has measured and described all three. Nearest the church is the biggest, a male whose trunk splits into four, 693 centimetres round at a foot off the ground in 1999. In 1874 the Gardener's Chronicle reported the bulkiest of the three at 24 feet. The middle one, also male, is a burnt-out hollow shell with ivy climbing into its crown, the hollow closing over above head height. The furthest, a female, is a ring of branches round the stump of the original trunk, 681 centimetres at the base. All three showed fire or smoke damage when they were surveyed in 1999.

In 1899 a visiting naturalist pronounced the great yew more than 2,000 years old. That was an opinion, not a measurement, and no modern survey has backed it. Nobody has dated these trees properly, so we leave the age open. If you know of a better estimate, tell us.

The churchyard is open and free, beside the village green in Tettenhall, a short bus ride west of Wolverhampton city centre. The ground on the north side is steep.

name: The Great Yew of Shugborough

location.address: Shugborough Estate, north of the house by the Temple, Milford, Stafford ST17

access: Paid entry. National Trust Shugborough Estate, entry through the Milford Gates only. On a sample date in November 2026 the garden and parkland were open 09:00 to 16:00; check the Trust's page for current hours and prices. Dogs on leads.
transport: Train to Stafford, then a bus towards Milford; the National Trust gives 10 to 30 minutes by bus from Stafford. From Wolverhampton this is a day out rather than a quick trip.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the huge yew that grows sideways in a tangle of rooted branches instead of a single tall trunk. It stands by the Temple just north of the house, on the north side of the lawn called The Flat.

photo.note: Not searched beyond Wikipedia/Commons-free check; AYG photos (Tim Hills 2009, D. Alderman) are copyrighted.

verify_notes: Ancient Yew Group tree 2001, class 'Notable', girth 373 cm (no measurement date or height given in database). Site Shugborough, parkland, access Public, grid ref SJ99232257, coordinates 52.800688 -2.0128618 (map link, site level); AYG says the yew stands by the Temple, just north of the house. Reputed 'Widest Tree in Europe'; the National Trust itself says its walled garden includes 'Europe's widest yew tree'. AYG notes it has grown into such a tangle that the main stem is almost impossible to reach, and describes it as a female yew that seems to grow sideways. Measurements recorded in the AYG entry: 1898 (John Lowe, Garden Magazine) girth 10 ft 2 in at 3 ft, height 42 ft, spread diameter 87 ft, circumference 261 ft, age then estimated 250 to 300 years; 1992 (Baxter, The Eternal Yew) girth 12 ft 3 in, height 71 ft, crown circumference 560 ft (about 171 m). A 1925 entry ticket attributes the wide spread to branches rooting and young shoots growing rapidly after rooting. A more recent source cited by AYG suggests a planting date around 1700; not independently seen, so no age adopted. Girth 373 cm equals 12 ft 3 in, consistent with Baxter 1992. Alive: Express and Star 28 Jan 2020 reports volunteers pruning the Great Yew (search result title only; page 403 to fetch) and the National Trust still advertises it. Superlative: 'widest in Europe' is a reputation, not a measurement; Tree Register of the British Isles reportedly records the largest crown in Britain and Ireland (seen only in a search summary, not fetched, so unverified; do not cite). Estate returned to the National Trust management in 2016 (Wikipedia). The AYG notes also say 'Staffordshire County Council finances the estate', which is out of date. Whether the tree is inside the paid-entry area or the free parkland is not stated on a fetched page; treat as paid.
story:
The National Trust says Shugborough's garden holds Europe's widest yew, and the way it got wide is the story. This yew grows sideways. A visitor's ticket from 1925 already gave the reason. Its branches bend to the ground, root where they touch and send up fast young shoots, so over the years it has spread into a tangle so dense that, the Ancient Yew Group notes, its main stem is almost impossible to reach.

The measurements show the spread. In 1898 a survey gave the crown a circumference of 261 feet. By 1992 it was given as 560 feet, about 171 metres round. The trunk itself is modest by comparison, 373 centimetres round. An 1898 writer guessed the tree was then 250 to 300 years old, and a later source has suggested planting around 1700. We have not seen the evidence for either, so we leave the age open. Widest in Europe is the Trust's claim and the tree's reputation, not the result of a measured contest.

It is a female tree, and it stands by the Temple just north of the house, on the north side of the lawn known as The Flat. Shugborough is National Trust land on the edge of Cannock Chase, with paid entry to the park and gardens through the Milford Gates. The Trust still shows it to visitors as one of the garden's sights.

name: Groot Tree, Brocton Coppice

location.address: Brocton Coppice, Cannock Chase, near Brocton, Stafford ST17

access: Free. Brocton Coppice is open woodland on Cannock Chase, protected as a Site of Special Scientific Interest and Special Area of Conservation; keep to the paths and bridleways. Walks start from the Coppice Hill car park in Brocton.
transport: Brocton is about five miles from Stafford. The Chase is mostly reached by car; public transport to the car park is not confirmed.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its gnarled, knotted trunk, which walkers say looks like Groot from Guardians of the Galaxy. It stands among the ancient oaks of Brocton Coppice, where the old oaks stand out against the birch.
verify_notes: Geograph photo 7023610 'Groot Tree, Brockton Coppice, Cannock Chase', Brian Deegan, CC BY-SA 2.0, taken 20 Nov 2021; his description: 'Old Oak Tree, maybe 500+ years old' (an amateur caption, not a survey). Subject grid SJ 9843 1995 = WGS84 52.77713 -2.02471, camera SJ 9844 1998. OpenStreetMap node 12776476313 (added 25 Apr 2025 by Reino Baptista) 'Groot Tree', natural=tree, dominant_taxon Quercus robur, tag fixme='exact location tbc', website pointing at the Geograph photo, so it descends from the same photograph and is NOT independent coordinate evidence; coordinates 52.7771330 -2.0247130. Komoot highlight 4432792 (Natural Monument, 4.9 from 39 ratings) 'Groot Tree', tip by Kenny dated 6 Sep 2023: 'An old tree which resembles Groot'; map link 52.77759 -2.024921 (about 40 m from the OSM point, so the exact trunk is uncertain within some tens of metres). Alive: Geograph Nov 2021, Komoot Sep 2023, OSM Apr 2025. Species: OSM says Quercus robur, but Staffordshire County Council and the Cannock Chase site describe the Coppice oaks as sessile; neither verified for this tree, so species left as Oak (Quercus sp.). Context for the writer: Brocton Coppice is a 200-acre woodland with about 600 sessile oaks and the highest concentration of ancient and veteran trees in Staffordshire (Cannock Chase heritage page and a Staffordshire County Council statement quoted in search results, with 'some over 500 years old' and 'remnant of the royal hunting forest of Cank'); illegal bike trails damaged oak roots (Staffordshire County Council, Feb 2021). The Coppice-wide numbers are from search summaries of the county council pages and the Cannock Chase heritage page text only partly seen (the fetched Cannock Chase page confirms the highest concentration of ancient and veteran trees in Staffordshire and oak mining bees, nothing on ages), so use only the highest-concentration claim as sourced. Another Treebeard-like oak in the Sher Brook Valley near the stepping stones was reported by Staffordshire Live (page not fetchable); lead only. Hard rule: this is one amateur-named trunk; the 500+ age is one caption. Ship as a lone tree page with the recognition line, not a city. Photo held (writing pass 2026-11-03): the Groot trunk is clearly visible mid-frame, but the picture is dusk-dark, photo_light POOR (underexposed, flat), and a large unrelated trunk dominates the left third. A brighter photograph wins.
story:
Walkers on Cannock Chase named this oak after Groot, the walking tree from Guardians of the Galaxy, and the old, gnarled trunk explains it. It is the sort of tree you half expect to turn round.

It grows in Brocton Coppice, which holds the highest concentration of ancient and veteran trees in Staffordshire. The Coppice is old oak woodland with birch around it, on ground that is protected for its wildlife twice over, as a Site of Special Scientific Interest and a Special Area of Conservation.

How old this one is, nobody knows. The photographer who posted it under that name in 2021 guessed 500 years or more, and that is a caption, not a survey. We have not settled the species either. One map record calls it a pedunculate oak, while the Coppice's own oaks are described as sessile, so if you know your acorns, tell us which.

The tree has been photographed in 2021, described on a walking app in 2023 and mapped in 2025, so it is very much standing. Its exact position is less certain. The records we have disagree by some tens of metres, so walk in from the Coppice Hill car park and look for the oak that looks back. Stay on the paths. Brocton Coppice is free and open.

name: Codsall Churchyard Yews

location.address: St Nicholas churchyard, Church Road, Codsall, Wolverhampton WV8

transport: Train from Wolverhampton to Codsall station on the Shrewsbury line, then a short walk to the church.

location_site.name: St Nicholas churchyard, south-east side of the church

how_to_recognise: You can recognise them as the two old yews south-east of the church. The larger, to the east-south-east, is a two-sided mass of twiggy growth; the smaller, to the south-east, is the remaining shell of a once larger tree.

photo.note: AYG photos (Tim Hills 2003, Tony Hackett 2005) are copyright. No open photo searched.

verify_notes: Ancient Yew Group site record, St Nicholas Codsall, Lichfield diocese, grid ref SJ86620403, coordinates 52.633853 -2.1991334 (site-level map link). Visited 31 March 2003 by Tim Hills; 2019 site file. Two yews: tree 1516 female, Ancient 5-7m, 589 cm at 5 cm (19 ft 4 in close to the ground, 2003), grows ESE of the church, 'a tree of two distinct sides, each covered in adventitious growth and twiggy branches'; tree 1517 male, Ancient 4-5m, 399 cm (13 ft 1 in) close to the ground (2003), grows SE of the church, 'has been larger and all that remains is a sizeable fragment of its shell'. History quoted in the AYG file: 1801 History and Antiquities of Staffordshire (Rev. Stebbing Shaw) described the yews as 'very ancient' and possibly from the time of the 13th-century tower; 1899 Lynam wrote of 'its ancient tower, its more ancient yew tree'. Church earliest part Norman (AYG). Single source family (AYG with its historic citations), no independent second source and no vitality check later than 2005 photos, so flagged: alive is NOT confirmed within recent years. Churchyard is public and managed by South Staffordshire Council. Two trees within one churchyard fold into one collectible point. Weaker than Tettenhall; ship only if the place needs the count.
story:
In 1801 a county historian already called the Codsall yews very ancient and wondered whether they were as old as the church's 13th-century tower. In 1899 another writer went further, praising Codsall's ancient tower and its more ancient yew tree. Nobody since has put a number on them, and we will not either.

There are two, both south-east of St Nicholas church. The larger is a female, 589 centimetres round close to the ground when the Ancient Yew Group measured it in 2003. It is a tree of two distinct sides, each thick with small shoots and twiggy branches. The smaller is a male, 399 centimetres round, and it is what is left of something bigger, a sizeable fragment of the shell of a once larger tree.

The church's earliest parts are Norman, so a churchyard has stood here for a very long time. Whether the yews go back that far is the open question.

The most recent records we have are photographs from 2005. We believe both trees still stand, but if you visit, tell us what you find. The churchyard is open, a short walk from the centre of Codsall, a village on the railway line north-west of Wolverhampton with its own station.
